How this book matches your exam. This book follows the new IB Psychology guide (first assessment 2027). The course is built on:

  • concepts: bias, causality, change, measurement, perspective, responsibility;
  • content: the biological, cognitive and sociocultural approaches, and research methods;
  • contexts: health and well-being, human development, human relationships, learning and cognition.

This book covers the biological approach:

  • localisation;
  • neuroplasticity;
  • neurotransmitters;
  • brain-imaging techniques;
  • hormones;
  • genetics (twin studies and gene–environment interaction);
  • animal research.

Unit 1 of 10: The Biological Approach and the Six Concepts

Key ideas

  • The biological approach: behaviour and mental processes are influenced by the brain, the nervous system, hormones and genes.
  • Its assumptions:
  • there are biological correlates of behaviour;
  • animal research can tell us about humans;
  • behaviour can be inherited (genetics).
  • The six concepts applied:
  • causality: can we say the brain causes behaviour, or is the data correlational?
  • measurement: how valid are brain scans and hormone levels as measures?
  • change: neuroplasticity;
  • bias: reductionism; samples;
  • perspective: biological versus other explanations;
  • responsibility: the ethics of animal and genetic research.

Worked examples

Example 1: finding a larger hippocampus in taxi drivers shows a correlation; it does not prove that driving caused the change (causality).

Example 2: fMRI measures blood oxygen, not neurons directly (a measurement issue).

Example 3: explaining depression only through serotonin is reductionist (a bias and perspective issue).

10-mark exam-style question

(a) Outline two assumptions of the biological approach. [4]

(b) Explain how the concept of causality applies to biological research. [6]

Answers:

  • (a) Behaviour has biological correlates in the brain, the hormones and the genes (A2). Animal research can be generalised to humans because they share biological structures (A2).
  • (b) Many biological studies are correlational (brain scans, twin studies), so they cannot establish cause and effect (R2). Experiments (for example, drug manipulations of neurotransmitters) allow stronger causal claims, because the independent variable is manipulated under controlled conditions (R2). Even then, causality may be bidirectional (behaviour changes the brain), as neuroplasticity shows (R2).

Common mistakes

  1. Assuming that correlation means causation.
  2. Ignoring the bidirectional relationship.
  3. Using the concepts as labels with no explanation.
  4. Ignoring the other approaches.
  5. Overgeneralising from animals.

Quick recall

  1. Name the six concepts.
  2. What does the biological approach study?
  3. What is reductionism?
  4. Are brain scans experimental or correlational?
  5. Give one ethical issue in biological research.

Answers: 1) Bias, causality, change, measurement, perspective, responsibility. 2) The brain, hormones and genes. 3) Explaining complex behaviour by its simplest parts. 4) Usually correlational. 5) Harm to animals.
